seriesTitle: The Lantern Mender of Pell Street
title: Pretty Glass
blurb: Ada finds Tobias at the top of the clock tower, unsure of his own name, and a ferryman opens a tin of pretty glass.

blocks.text: Eighty-nine. Ninety. Ninety-one.
Ada counted the iron stairs under her breath, because counting was better than thinking. Above her, somewhere among the wheels, someone was tapping. Three short. One long.
At the top the wind sang through the louvres. A man stood in the brown brass with one finger on a gear, and turned to her as politely as a stranger.
"Do I know you?" said Tobias. "I think I fix clocks. Is that right?"
"Your name is Tobias Penhallow," said Ada. "Say it back to me."
He opened his mouth. Nothing came out of it.
He frowned at the gear instead, as if it had asked. "Five hours to first bell," he said. "Give or take. Don't know how I know that."
Ada knew. People forgot the who and kept the how. Odile still set two cups. Tobias still knew the time with the clock stopped.

She had been looking for him since ninth bell: the market, the bridges, the steps, every doorway on the square, her red hands stinging in the cold. The tower door had been shut when she tried it first. Now it stood open. His feet had brought him back to the only work they knew.
"You're a clockmaker," she said. "You call the clock 'her'. You grumble before you do anyone a kindness. Come down with me."
"Why?"
"Because somebody broke your lantern, and I'm the only one who can mend it, and I need you standing behind me with your hands in your pockets."
He looked at his hands as if they were somebody else's. Then he put them in his pockets.
Rain had come on. Odile was waiting in the doorway of the clock shop under her green umbrella, and beside her, buttoned to the throat, with the Register under his arm, stood Emrys.
"I fetched him," said Odile, before Ada could speak. "You were talking to an empty shop, Ada, saying a name over and over, and I thought, well, either she's tired or she's—"
"I'm not."
"—hungry, I was going to say hungry." Odile looked past her at Tobias, kind and blank. "Hello there. Are you lost?"
Tobias tapped the doorframe. Three short, one long. He said nothing.
"This is Tobias Penhallow," said Ada. "This is his shop. He's been rebuilding the tower clock for ten years. That's his wheel on the bench."
Emrys did not look at Tobias. He took his spectacles off and looked at Ada.
"The Register," he said, "is the—it is meant to be the last word on who lives where. For the record."
He set it on the bench beside the glass and the bright sixty-tooth wheel, and turned the brown pages to the square. His finger went down the lines. The hall. The bell tower. Under the tower.
Under the tower, the line was blank.
"Empty since ever," said Odile softly. "I said."
Emrys took a folded sheet from inside his coat, his tally, and read down it twice.
"This one isn't on here," he said. "Every blank in that book is on this sheet, with the date I found it. Not this one. So either I missed a line, which I do not, or it went blank tonight."
"At ninth bell," said Ada. "Somebody broke his lantern on this bench."

"A blank line says nobody is there. It doesn't say who isn't." He looked at Tobias at last, a long look, as if Tobias were a margin he could not quite read. "You're asking me to put a name to a blank on your word alone. No ink. No witness. A shop my neighbour swears is empty."
"Yes."
The rain ticked on the window. Tobias tapped.
Then Emrys took the pencil from behind his ear and wrote at the foot of the tally, small and square: *Penhallow, T. Clock shop, under the tower. On the Mender's word.*
"This book has been wrong twelve times," he said. "Thirteen, now. You have not."
Odile took the pins out of her mouth, which she only did for serious things. "Well. If he believes you, I'll believe you louder. What do you need?"

Ada tipped the bench glass into her handkerchief. Not enough. She had known it at ninth bell, before her hands stopped shaking: the line of light had started across these pieces, joined a few, and broken off partway, and the bar had not come up at all. Not one shard missing. Half a lantern.
"The rest went in the water," she said. "Ines's did. Whoever does this likes the canal."
Emrys took one step back from the door, though the canal was a street away.
"I'll take the ferry," said Ada. "You two go round by the bridge. Light my lamp. Get the stove going."
The bow lantern came out of the rain like a slow star. Ada heard the oars before she saw them. Dip. Creak. Drip.
"Evening," said Old Nobody, bringing the flat black boat in against the Pell Street steps. "Or morning. One of the two. What's your name?"
"Ada."
"Ada." He nodded, as if filing it somewhere. "And his?"
Tobias opened his mouth.
"Tobias," said Ada.
"Tobias. Good name. Solid. Mind the step, Tobias, it's mostly weed."
They sat. The water slapped the hull. Ada asked whether he had seen anyone throw glass into the canal tonight.

"Glass." He shipped his oars. "I fish up glass. Have done for years. Pretty glass." From the bow, beside the lantern, he lifted a square biscuit tin, dented, its paint gone dull. "Came up a lot tonight, off the steps below the square. Sorry. What did you say your name was?"
"Ada."
"Ada. Ada." He prised the lid off.
Inside the lid a paper was pasted, in a hand that leaned hard to the right. *1. Pretty glass. 2. Keep it dry. 3. Somebody will want it.* Every line underlined twice.
The tin was full of years: green glass, brown glass, clear glass, all rubbed soft by the water. And on top, sharp-edged and still wet, curved pieces that caught the bow light.

Ada laid them on her knee beside the handkerchief. The readout came up gold in the dark. The line of light ran from piece to piece, the bench ones and the wet ones, edge to edge, all the way along. Then it ran off the last piece, out over the water, and stopped. Pointing at nothing.
INCOMPLETE, beneath the tier. The bar came up empty, with a notch cut from its far end.
Every piece but the last. Same as Ines. *The last shard keeps the last hand.*
"That's mine," said Tobias. His first words since the tower. "Feels like mine."
"It's yours."
Old Nobody watched her wrap them, and then he held out the whole tin.
"Somebody will want it," he said, as if reading off the lid. "Always thought somebody would. Bring it back. I'll forget I lent it, mind." He smiled, apologetic. "What's your name?"
That was twice. She did not mind it.
"Ada," she said. "Ada Brannock. The shop on Pell Street."
"Pell Street," he said, and picked up his oars. "I know Pell Street."
The shop lamp was lit, the stove ticking. Odile had gone for bread, Emrys said, because nobody should be remembered on an empty stomach.
"Time?" said Ada.
Tobias, hands in his pockets, tilted his head as if listening to a clock nobody else could hear. "Two hours. Less."

She laid the pieces out on the bench in the order the light gave them. Emrys stood at the end with the Register open at the square, and did not speak, which was the most useful thing anyone had done for her all night.
Test before you touch. She touched.

The glass clicked under her fingers, warm, warmer than any flame could make it. The bar crept. Pieces drew together like iron filings to a magnet, the base, the curve, the crown. Her palms, still tender from the tower, throbbed in time.
"Hour and a quarter," said Tobias.
She kept going.

Then the shop went away, and she was on the long quay in the dark. Water knee-high and rising. Every lamp dead. Shouting. The split of timber overhead, and the small dark-haired woman turning towards the sound, the dimple, the wide mouth. Ines. She knew the face now. Young hands struck between the shoulders, and Ines went back into the canal—
And there it stopped. Not ending. Torn, like a page ripped out of a book. At the ragged edge, for a heartbeat, Ada saw a dark glove, fingers closing.
Nothing else.
"Half an hour," said Tobias, very low. "Half past too late, if you stop."
She did not stop. One-two-three, under her breath, all the way to sixty, and again. The bar crawled to the notch, and touched it, and INCOMPLETE flickered once, and the readout faded.
Across the water, first bell rang. Deep and slow.
On the bench stood a lantern, whole except for a ragged gap the size of a thumbnail, low on one side. A small flame burned inside it, low and steady.
Emrys made a sound. On the page under his hand, on the blank line under the tower, soft brown ink was writing itself, old ink, not his hand: *Penhallow, Tobias. Clock shop, under the tower.*
"Eleven," Emrys said quietly. "Eleven blanks again."
Tobias took his hands out of his pockets.
"Tobias Penhallow," he said, to nobody, before anyone could ask. "Clocks. She's a wheel off." He rubbed his face. "Somebody came in at dusk. I had my back to the door. That's where it stops."
Ada nodded. She was busy.

*You won't feel it leave.* So she went looking, the way she always did now. Four digits. The postbox. The van. Then the place she never went: the dark ward, the generator coming up too slow, the bed in bay four.
She knew there had been a face on that pillow. She knew she had looked at it every night since, whether she meant to or not.
She could not see it. The face was gone. The guilt was not. It sat where the face had been, the same weight, holding nothing.
"Ada?" said Emrys.
"Later," she said.
He looked at her a long moment. Then he closed the Register, and went to tell Odile that she had a neighbour she had forgotten she remembered.
Ada wrote it on the brown paper while the light came up grey. *5. The face.* She did not write whose.
Tobias was at the door with his lantern under his coat when boots came up the Pell Street steps, slow, and a long kind creased face looked in.
"Only me," said Old Nobody. "Come for my tin. No—I lent it. Did I? I like to look in at first bell. See the light's out in here. Silly. In case somebody's left a job open."
Tobias went very still.
"Morning, Barnaby," he said.
The ferryman smiled politely. "Is that my name? People don't use it."
Tobias turned to Ada, and said it plainly, the way nobody in Morrow Quay had said it in two years.
"That's Barnaby Kestle. He was the Mender."
Ada took the ledger from the drawer and opened it at RULES. FOR WHOEVER COMES NEXT. She set the tin lid beside it.
The same hard lean to the right. The same numbers. The same underlining, pressed so deep the nib had bitten the paper. *Somebody will want it.* *Write down what goes.* One hand, a whole life apart.
"Every mend took a bit," said Tobias, low. "Names first. Then the rest. Two years back he came down those steps and asked me who he was. Town says the old Mender's gone. Kinder than saying where."
Barnaby was looking round the shop with mild interest. "Nice shop," he said. "I like the smell."
Ada looked at him, and at the ledger, and understood where the road went. Not into the fog. Here. A kind man in a good coat, mostly mending, looking in on his own shop like a stranger.
He rowed her out because she asked. She did not say why, and he did not ask. Along Pell Street someone was putting out the lamps one by one, and the sound of humming came down over the water. Hester.
Ada took the brown paper from her pocket and read it aloud.
"One. Mum's phone number. Two. My knee. How. Three. The way home from the station. The last turn. Four. His name. The man in the van. Five. The face."
Barnaby rowed. Dip. Creak.
"That's a list," he said kindly. "What's your name?"
"Ada."
"Ada." The oars dripped. "Sorry. What was it?"
"Ada," she said.

Five lines, and she had hardly been here any time at all. She could do the sum. She was an electrician; she always did the sum. At the far end of it was a boat, and a polite question, and nobody left inside to answer.
And Tobias was up his tower by now, remembered, with his wheel.
"I'm going to keep going," she said, to the water.
"Good," said Barnaby, who did not know what she meant. "Somebody should."
The boat bumped the steps. Ada caught at the edge of the seat to steady herself, and under it her fingers found paper, taped flat, the tape gone brown and brittle with years.
She peeled it free. The same hand, but younger, harder, surer, underlined so deep the nib had torn through:
*Ask who lit the lamps on Flood Night.*
